questions.q: What is an automation "collision," as this lesson defines it?
options: A Salesforce error that always prevents a save
A validation rule with a syntax error
Any time two approval processes exist in the same org
Two or more pieces of automation acting on the same save in an order the admin didn't fully anticipate, producing unexpected behavior
questions.explain: A collision isn't one broken component, it's the unmapped interaction between multiple automations touching the same save.

questions.q: According to the Apex Developer Guide, how many additional times can a workflow rule's field update re-trigger a save?
options: Exactly one additional time
Unlimited times, until a governor limit is hit
It depends on how many workflow rules exist on the object
Zero times; field updates never cause a re-save
questions.explain: A workflow field update forces one additional re-save, re-running before/after triggers and system validation, but it does not cascade further from workflow rules alone.

questions.q: During a recursive save, which of these is skipped according to Salesforce's documented behavior?
options: Assignment rules, auto-response rules, workflow rules, escalation rules, Process Builder/flows, and roll-up summary updates
System validation
The initial record load
Before triggers
questions.explain: Salesforce explicitly documents that a recursive save skips steps 9 through 17 of the order of execution, which covers that whole group.

questions.q: Do Apex triggers and Flow have the same automatic recursion ceiling that workflow field updates have?
options: No, a trigger or Flow without a recursion guard can run until it hits a governor limit
Yes, but only for Flow, not for Apex
Yes, every automation type is capped at exactly one re-save automatically
No, Apex and Flow are blocked from ever updating their own triggering record
questions.explain: Unlike the workflow field update safeguard, Apex triggers and Flow don't have a built-in recursion ceiling, so a missing guard can run until it hits a governor limit.

questions.q: Which practice most directly reduces the risk of a field-level collision between two automations?
options: Renaming all Flows to start with the same prefix
Deactivating all approval processes
Adding more validation rules to the same object
Documenting which fields each automation reads and writes
questions.explain: Two automations writing the same field without anyone realizing it is the most common collision source; documenting reads and writes surfaces that risk before it causes a problem.
